scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: An induction cooktop has no flame, and the glass beside the pan stays fairly cool. Yet the pan boils water fast. How?

scenes.name: coil
scenes.text: Under the glass is a coil of copper wire. Fast alternating current flows through it, tens of thousands of times a second.

scenes.name: field
scenes.text: That creates a magnetic field that keeps flipping direction, passing straight up through the glass.

scenes.name: eddy
scenes.text: The changing field induces swirling electric currents inside the metal base of the pan, called eddy currents.

scenes.name: heat
scenes.text: The metal resists those currents, turning that energy into heat. So the pan itself becomes the heater, not the glass.

scenes.name: pan
scenes.text: It needs a magnetic pan, like cast iron or many steel ones. If a magnet sticks to the bottom, it'll work.

scenes.name: eff
scenes.text: Most of the energy goes straight into the pan, with far less wasted heating the air than a gas flame.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Coil, field, currents, heat. Cooking with magnetism. Follow for more on how things really work.
